stories.headline: Puerto Rico Begins Emergency Water Rationing as Severe Drought Strains Aging Infrastructure
stories.summary:
Puerto Rico launched mandatory water rationing Friday across major cities, with residents subject to rotating 48-hour shutoffs as a severe drought depletes the island's reservoirs. Governor Jenniffer González-Colón issued a public plea urging conservation, asking residents to turn off taps while washing and showering. The island-wide rationing marks a significant escalation of a water crisis that has left some communities without reliable service for more than a year.

The rollout has been marked by confusion, with some households receiving water during periods they were scheduled to go without, and others in ongoing blackout zones still lacking service. Investigative reporters on the ground described a breakdown in government communication, with residents uncertain about when and whether their water would be restored. Public health concerns are mounting over the prospect of extended interruptions in densely populated areas.

Officials and journalists say the drought has exposed long-standing failures in Puerto Rico's water infrastructure, which has struggled since Hurricane Maria caused catastrophic damage in 2017. Underfunding of the Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority and delayed repairs have left the system vulnerable to climatic stress. Critics argue that the crisis was foreseeable and that government inaction compounded the impact of natural conditions.

The situation affects all 3.2 million residents of the island, raising concerns about water access for hospitals, schools, and vulnerable populations. No immediate federal emergency declaration has been announced, and it remains unclear when reservoir levels could recover sufficiently to end rationing.

stories.headline: Hunter Biden Says Presidential Pardon Was 'Not Good' for America or His Father's Legacy
stories.summary:
In a wide-ranging interview with BBC Newsnight, Hunter Biden acknowledged that the full pardon granted to him by his father, former President Joe Biden, in December 2024 was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution, or his father's legacy. He said he understood the criticism but questioned how his father could have done otherwise: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me." He added that he and his father never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

Hunter Biden said the elder Biden acted out of fear that his son would become a political target under the incoming Trump administration. The pardon covered Hunter Biden's federal gun conviction, a tax case he pleaded guilty to, and any federal offenses committed between 2014 and 2024 — a scope that drew widespread bipartisan criticism at the time, given President Biden's repeated prior assurances that he would not intervene in his son's legal cases.

In the interview, Hunter Biden also disclosed new details about his father's health, saying that former President Biden's prostate cancer "has spread, metastasised into his bones and further" and is "very painful" and "very debilitating." He described his father as still the center of the family but acknowledged the disease is taking a significant toll.

Hunter Biden also described the depths of his addiction — drinking nearly a gallon of vodka daily and smoking crack cocaine almost every 15 minutes at its worst — calling it "hell on earth." He ruled out seeking elected office and said he is focused on advocacy for addiction recovery.

stories.headline: Sen. Cassidy Backs Todd Blanche for Attorney General, Potentially Reviving Stalled Nomination
stories.summary:
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana announced on the Senate floor Friday that he will support Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general, a move that could prove pivotal after two Republican senators — Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine — came out in opposition and threw the confirmation into doubt. Cassidy acknowledged that Blanche "is not perfect" but argued that any alternative nominee might not be an improvement.

Blanche, a former private attorney who represented President Trump in multiple criminal cases, was nominated to lead the Justice Department. His nomination has drawn scrutiny from some Republicans over concerns about his qualifications and independence, while Democrats have raised broader objections about conflicts of interest given his prior representation of the sitting president.

Cassidy's announcement reflects the narrow margin Republicans hold in the Senate and the difficulty of confirming nominees when any two members of the majority defect. With Murkowski and Collins opposed, the math remains tight and it is unclear whether Blanche has secured sufficient votes for confirmation.

The nomination fight comes amid broader tensions at the Justice Department, including separate controversies Friday over the Pentagon revoking former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall's security clearance — alleging he disclosed classified information to media about the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One — and ongoing disputes over DOJ press subpoenas that were subsequently withdrawn after judicial criticism.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Warns Tehran of 'Last Chance' as Iran War Negotiations Resume
stories.summary:
President Trump issued a stark warning to Iran on Friday, declaring it has a "last chance" to reach a deal as diplomatic back-channel activity intensified around the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Qatar announced that mediators were making progress toward ending the war, though Tehran publicly denied Trump's assertion that formal talks were already underway — a sign of the competing narratives surrounding the negotiations.

Analysts at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies warned that Iran is deliberately escalating political pressure to gain diplomatic leverage, noting that the regime has historically been willing to gamble at the edge of confrontation. One senior Iran analyst argued that while Trump has inflicted more damage on the Iranian regime than any prior U.S. president, recent pullbacks from earlier threats have allowed Tehran to portray Washington as a "paper tiger" in state-aligned media.

The story is covered by 23 outlets across the political spectrum, making it the most widely sourced story of the day. It represents a material new development in the ongoing Iran conflict: a direct presidential ultimatum combined with Qatari mediation progress and Tehran's public denial, shifting the diplomatic dynamic significantly from prior days.

The right frames Trump's warning as necessary resolve to force a capitulation from a weakened regime; the left and some centrist analysts caution that the mixed signals — threats followed by pullbacks — risk undermining U.S. credibility and could embolden Iran to stall further.

stories.headline: Update: White House Launches Second Attempt to Remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has initiated a new effort to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, sending her a formal letter notifying her that the president is "considering" her removal over mortgage fraud allegations and giving her 21 days to respond. The move comes after the Supreme Court this year blocked Trump's first removal attempt, ruling Cook was not given proper notice or an opportunity to respond — procedural defects the new letter seeks to remedy.

The action is widely seen as an unprecedented challenge to Federal Reserve independence. The Supreme Court's earlier ruling explicitly upheld the Fed's independence, and legal experts say it remains uncertain whether satisfying the notice requirement will be sufficient to overcome that protection. Cook, an economist and the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor, has not publicly commented on the new letter.

Supporters of the administration argue Cook's alleged mortgage fraud conduct disqualifies her from her post and that the president has legitimate removal authority over executive branch officials. Critics contend the real motivation is Trump's long-running frustration with Fed interest-rate policy and that removing a sitting governor would fundamentally undermine the central bank's political independence, potentially rattling financial markets.

The story is a concrete new development — a second formal removal proceeding — on a previously covered clash between the White House and the Federal Reserve.

stories.headline: Spain and Algeria Bust One of Western Mediterranean's Largest Smuggling Networks, 78 Arrested
stories.summary:
Spanish police and Algerian authorities, in coordination with Europol, dismantled what officials described as one of the largest criminal smuggling networks operating in the western Mediterranean, arresting 78 people across 17 locations in Spain and in Algeria. The network trafficked synthetic drugs outbound from Spain and Portugal to Algeria and used return voyages to smuggle migrants and weapons into Spain on unregistered high-speed "ghost speedboats."

Authorities seized 18 high-powered vessels valued at €5 million, firearms, encrypted communications equipment, and 15,000 MDMA pills. Europol said profits from migrant smuggling alone exceeded €24 million, with the network charging up to €12,000 per person and moving more than 50 migrants per trip, often in overcrowded boats without lights or life jackets. Investigators also allege sexual assaults and physical abuse of migrants held in makeshift housing.

The bust is notable for its scale and its dual-flow structure — the network served as logistics infrastructure for multiple other criminal organizations across France, Belgium, Portugal, Italy, and Poland, making it a significant node in broader European organized crime. The announcement comes days after a separate mass crossing incident at Ceuta, underlining the intensity of migration pressure on Spain's borders.

The operation was led by Spanish National Police with Europol coordination, with suspects primarily of Algerian origin. No group has claimed political motivation; authorities characterize it as profit-driven organized crime.

stories.headline: Fired Federal Prosecutor Sues Justice Department, Alleging Wrongful Dismissal After Right-Wing Influencer's Accusation
stories.summary:
A former federal prosecutor, Will Rosenzweig, filed suit against the Justice Department on Friday alleging he was unlawfully dismissed after a right-wing media figure publicly accused him of political bias, according to the New York Times. Rosenzweig joins a growing roster of former prosecutors and federal agents who have turned to the courts to contest what critics describe as a politically motivated purge of career law enforcement officials deemed insufficiently loyal to the current administration.

The lawsuit adds to a pattern of legal challenges from within the Justice Department's career ranks. Several former officials have alleged that firings were triggered not by documented misconduct but by complaints from partisan media figures or political appointees, raising due-process concerns. The DOJ has not publicly commented on Rosenzweig's specific case.

Supporters of the administration argue that the president has broad authority to shape the composition of federal law enforcement and that career officials who openly resisted administration priorities warranted removal. Critics, including former prosecutors across party lines, contend the firings undermine prosecutorial independence and the rule of law.

The case is covered by two outlets with differing perspectives — the New York Times and the Washington Examiner — providing left-leaning and right-leaning framing respectively, and represents a fresh legal filing today rather than a continuation of previously reported events.

stories.headline: Don Lemon Asks Judge to Dismiss Federal Charges, Alleging Vindictive Prosecution by Trump DOJ
stories.summary:
Former CNN anchor Don Lemon filed a motion Friday asking a federal judge to dismiss a felony indictment stemming from his coverage of an anti-immigration enforcement protest at a church in St. Paul, Minnesota, earlier this year. His lawyers argue that the Trump Justice Department selectively and vindictively targeted him because of President Trump's personal animus toward the journalist, calling the charges "unprecedented" for a reporter doing his job.

Prosecutors allege Lemon participated in a "takeover-style attack" at Cities Church in St. Paul during an anti-ICE demonstration and have charged him accordingly. The government contends his conduct crossed the line from journalism into criminal participation. Lemon's legal team disputes that characterization entirely, asserting he was present in a reporting capacity.

The case has drawn attention as one of several high-profile confrontations between the Trump administration and media figures or former law enforcement officials. Critics of the prosecution, including the Good Law Project and civil liberties advocates, say the charges represent an effort to chill press freedom. Supporters of the prosecution argue no individual, including journalists, is above the law when they allegedly engage in criminal conduct.

The motion for dismissal on selective and vindictive prosecution grounds is a high legal bar to clear, but legal experts say the case raises significant First Amendment and due process questions. A ruling on the motion could come within weeks and will be closely watched by press freedom organizations.

stories.headline: Mexico and Peru Restore Diplomatic Relations After Nine-Month Asylum Dispute
stories.summary:
Mexico and Peru announced Thursday they are re-establishing full diplomatic relations, ending a rupture that began in November 2025 when former Peruvian Prime Minister Betssy Chávez sought asylum in the Mexican embassy in Lima after being charged for her alleged role in a 2022 coup attempt. A joint statement cited "historic ties of brotherhood, friendship and cooperation" as the basis for reconciliation.

Under the agreement, Chávez was granted safe passage and has already departed Peru for Mexico, according to Peruvian Foreign Minister Carlos Espá. Peru retains the right to seek her eventual extradition. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum welcomed Chávez at her daily briefing and reiterated her government's support for former Peruvian President Pedro Castillo, who remains imprisoned in Peru after his own failed attempt to dissolve congress in December 2022.

The restoration of ties follows the inauguration last week of Peru's new president, Keiko Fujimori, whose administration took a less confrontational approach to the standoff than her predecessor. During the dispute, Peru had cut diplomatic ties with Mexico entirely and declared the Mexican president persona non grata in its congress.

The resolution removes a significant source of tension in Latin American diplomacy, where the competing principles of state sovereignty and asylum rights frequently come into conflict. Both governments reaffirmed their commitment to international law and the UN Charter in the joint statement.

stories.headline: Update: Michigan Eases Lettuce Warnings as Cyclospora Outbreak Shows Signs of Slowing
stories.summary:
Michigan health officials on Thursday lifted broad precautionary advisories against purchasing bagged salad mixes, saying new cases of cyclosporiasis and related emergency department visits are trending downward. The state had recorded 12,485 cases since June, making it one of the hardest-hit states in an outbreak that previously surpassed 20,000 suspected cases nationwide across nearly all U.S. states.

Residents are now advised to follow routine food safety guidance for produce rather than the sweeping lettuce avoidance recommendations issued at the height of the outbreak. Health officials did not declare the outbreak over but characterized the easing of restrictions as a positive sign that the worst may have passed in the state.

The cyclospora outbreak, caused by a microscopic parasite typically linked to fresh produce, has been one of the largest foodborne illness events in recent U.S. history. Federal investigators had been working to identify the precise source of contamination amid the unusually wide geographic spread of cases.

The Michigan development is the first significant public health rollback associated with the outbreak and may signal that other states could ease similar advisories in coming weeks if case counts continue to fall. Federal health authorities have not yet issued a national update on the status of the broader investigation.

stories.headline: ICE to Deploy Body Cameras Nationwide by September, But Policy Allows Selective Release of Footage
stories.summary:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced it will equip field officers nationwide with body-worn cameras by the end of September, ending years of delays. The rollout comes after a series of fatal shootings by ICE officers during President Trump's intensified immigration enforcement operations increased public pressure for accountability measures.

However, the agency's body camera policy gives ICE's director broad discretion over what footage is made public. Under the policy, video of shootings or encounters causing death or serious injury will only be released promptly if the director determines it is in the agency's "best interests." A review committee of senior ICE officials and lawyers will assess footage after serious incidents and recommend whether to release it, with the director retaining authority to block or indefinitely delay disclosure.

Experts on law enforcement transparency said the policy is unusual in making selective release so explicit. "ICE is saying the quiet part out loud," said Christopher Schneider of Brandon University, a co-author of a book on police body cameras. "Body-worn cameras are being used as contemporary image-work tools to present the police to the public in the most favorable way possible." Transparency advocates argue that the tens of millions of taxpayer dollars funding the cameras should come with an expectation of public accountability.

ICE did not respond to questions about how it would determine what circumstances justify withholding footage. Supporters of the policy argue that law enforcement agencies routinely manage the release of sensitive video to protect ongoing investigations and officer safety, and that ICE faces unique threats given the contentious nature of immigration enforcement operations.

stories.headline: U.S. Economy Sheds 23,000 Jobs in July, Badly Missing Forecasts
stories.summary:
The U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a dramatic miss against economist forecasts that had anticipated gains of roughly 83,000 to 95,000 positions. The unemployment rate dipped slightly to 4.1 percent, but job gains for the two prior months were also revised downward, compounding the disappointing picture. The report marks the second consecutive month of weak jobs data.

Officials and analysts attributed the shortfall in part to the ongoing energy supply shock stemming from the U.S. war with Iran, which has weighed on business hiring decisions. The miss is one of the largest against consensus forecasts in recent years and signals a potential broader economic slowdown.

Supporters of the administration's economic policies have pointed to the dip in the unemployment rate as a silver lining, while critics argue the job losses confirm that the Iran conflict and associated energy disruptions are inflicting real damage on American workers. The report is expected to intensify debate in Washington over the war's economic costs ahead of November midterm elections.

The Federal Reserve will be closely watching the data as it weighs its next move on interest rates. Markets reacted sharply to the report, which arrived with six outlets covering the story, making it one of the most widely corroborated economic news events of the day.

stories.headline: Thailand School Shooting Kills at Least 7, Wounds 15
stories.summary:
A teenage student in Thailand shot and killed his grandparents before opening fire at his high school on Friday, killing at least five staff members and wounding 15 others, according to Thai police. The shooter subsequently killed himself. Authorities described the suspect as a student who had been bullied and was considered troubled by classmates.

The attack occurred at a high school and is among the deadliest school shootings in Thailand's modern history. At least eight people total were killed, including the grandparents, and emergency responders treated the wounded at the scene.

The episode immediately reignited public debate in Thailand over gun laws and access to firearms. The country has relatively high rates of civilian gun ownership compared to other Southeast Asian nations, and previous mass shooting incidents — including a 2020 attack by a soldier that killed dozens — have prompted calls for tighter restrictions that have largely stalled in the legislature.

Three outlets are covering the story across left and center sources. No Thai government officials had issued a formal policy response as of the time of publication.

stories.headline: Trump Says Republican Voters Are Angry at Congress, Not at Him, as Midterms Near
stories.summary:
President Trump, in an interview published Friday, sought to deflect responsibility for rising discontent among Republican voters, arguing that GOP anger is directed at congressional Republicans rather than at him personally. "They're angry at Republicans but they're not angry at me," Trump told Punchbowl News. The comments come as Trump's approval rating has fallen into the 30s, according to polling cited by Axios, with the ongoing Iran war and its economic consequences weighing on public sentiment.

Republican leaders are separately planning a first-ever midterm convention in Dallas next month, aiming to shift the campaign narrative away from a referendum on Trump's presidency and toward an attack on Democrats as captive to their activist left wing. The strategy, described by Axios, reflects GOP concern that a pure Trump-focused election environment would disadvantage incumbents.

The party also faces internal headaches: a series of abuse and harassment allegations involving several House Republican members — including Reps. Max Miller of Ohio, Cory Mills of Florida, and Chuck Edwards of North Carolina — threaten to complicate the midterm message. Democrats have added 12 Republican-held districts to their target list with 90 days until the November 3 election.

Trump also attacked Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in public remarks Friday, signaling he intends to make the Michigan race a centerpiece of the fall campaign. Three outlets covered the broader story.

stories.headline: Zelensky Makes First Official Visit to Russia-Friendly Serbia
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will travel to Belgrade on Saturday for his first official visit to Serbia, one of the few European nations that has declined to join international sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. The visit was announced by Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić's office late Thursday. Zelensky's office had not officially confirmed the trip as of Friday.

Serbia occupies an unusual position in European geopolitics: it is formally pursuing EU membership but relies almost entirely on Russia for energy and has maintained historic and cultural ties with Moscow. Vučić has met Zelensky on prior occasions but has consistently refused to sign declarations endorsing tougher sanctions against Russia. He reaffirmed that position Friday, saying Serbia's stance "has not changed and this will remain so for the time being."

Analysts see the visit as mutually beneficial. Zelensky is described as signaling to Moscow that Ukraine is making inroads with traditional Russian allies in the Balkans, while Vučić is seeking to demonstrate to Brussels that Serbia shares European values on the war — a move potentially useful as Serbia's EU accession process faces stalling over its Russia ties and democratic backsliding.

The visit comes as Serbia's relationship with the EU is under strain. Brussels has warned Belgrade it could lose access to EU funds and faces a frozen membership bid partly because of its alignment with Moscow. Russia previously accused Serbia of exporting arms to Ukraine through NATO member states.

stories.headline: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan Sign Trilateral Defense Agreement
stories.summary:
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca on Friday, establishing a coordinated security posture among three of the Islamic world's most militarily significant nations. The signing brought together Turkish President Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The agreement was concluded against the backdrop of the ongoing Iran war, which has reshaped regional security calculations across the Middle East and South Asia.

The pact marks a significant realignment in regional geopolitics, uniting a NATO member (Turkey), a major Gulf Arab power, and the world's only Muslim-majority nuclear-armed state in a formal security framework. Each country has navigated the Iran conflict with varying degrees of distance from U.S.-led operations, making the trilateral arrangement notable for its independent character. Analysts are likely to scrutinize whether the agreement is defensive in nature or signals a broader effort to project collective influence in a rapidly shifting regional order.

The deal has implications well beyond the three signatories, potentially affecting NATO cohesion, Gulf Cooperation Council dynamics, and the posture of other regional actors including Israel and Iran. Pakistan's inclusion introduces a nuclear dimension to the arrangement. No details were immediately released on the specific terms of the agreement, including whether it includes mutual defense commitments or is limited to intelligence and operational coordination.

stories.headline: Update: UEFA Threatens World Cup Boycott as FIFA Crisis Deepens After Infantino Retains Post
stories.summary:
UEFA said Thursday that its call for a potential boycott of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, remains live after concluding that FIFA's internal meeting in Rabat failed to meet the conditions it had set for restoring confidence. The European governing body had demanded both a full withdrawal of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment proposal and binding assurances that no similar scheme would be attempted again. UEFA said neither condition had been satisfied, and that Infantino's retention of the presidency "changes nothing."

The English Football Association formally withdrew its support for Infantino in a letter, adding to the pressure on the 56-year-old Swiss-Italian executive. At the same time, South American confederation CONMEBOL, the Confederation of African Football, and the football associations of World Cup co-hosts Mexico and runners-up Argentina all expressed backing for Infantino, illustrating the deep split in global football governance. The FFE proposal had offered associations $40 million each in exchange for backing private investment in FIFA's major tournaments.

Infantino convened the FIFA management board meeting himself rather than appearing before it under pressure, and was subsequently photographed smiling alongside FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafstrom — who had previously criticized the FFE scheme in an internal memo — at a Women's Africa Cup of Nations match. The visible display of unity within FIFA headquarters contrasted sharply with the sustained opposition from European football's governing body. Whether UEFA will follow through on a boycott threat that would upend the 2030 World Cup remains the central unresolved question.

stories.headline: Update: Thousands of Migrants Remain in Ceuta as New Mass Crossing Calls Circulate Online
stories.summary:
Between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta following a mass crossing last week in which roughly 78,000 people arrived by sea from Morocco within hours, according to Ceuta's regional leader Juan Jesús Vivas. Approximately 75,000 have since been returned to Morocco, but Vivas told the European Parliament on Thursday that a humanitarian emergency and public order disruptions persist. He also warned that new calls for mass crossings are circulating on social media, according to Moroccan media.

Vivas, a conservative, was sharply critical of Spain's Socialist-led national government, saying Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had been warned repeatedly and that the response was "late and insufficient." The EU Commission, by contrast, commended Spain's handling of the crisis, including the deployment of armed forces to Ceuta and the nearby enclave of Melilla. The Spanish government has allocated €25 million to assist unaccompanied minors, but volunteer groups have registered nearly 4,860 migrant children in Ceuta — double official estimates — and no children have yet been transferred to mainland Spain.

The immediate trigger for last week's crossing was a Spanish Supreme Court ruling barring the summary return of migrants intercepted at sea near the enclaves. EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner attributed the surge to criminal networks spreading disinformation, a view shared by Sánchez. The crisis has exposed fault lines between Spain's central government and conservative local authorities, as well as broader tensions among EU member states over migration and border policy.

stories.headline: Russia Escalates Black Sea Attacks on Ukrainian Ports; July Deadliest Month for Merchant Shipping Since Invasion
stories.summary:
Russia has sharply intensified missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure, with July recording 57 attacks on civilian vessels and 67 strikes on port facilities, according to Ukraine's port administration. Lloyd's List, the global shipping journal, has identified the Black Sea as potentially the most dangerous waters for commercial shipping in the world, calling July the deadliest month for merchant seamen since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022. A Turkish-owned cargo ship, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles on July 19, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot before sinking off Odesa.

The campaign is targeting Ukraine's primary commercial lifelines — the ports of Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi — with the aim of severing the country's agricultural and commercial exports. Port workers in Odesa describe conditions under which missile flight times from Russian-occupied Crimea are shorter than the time needed to evacuate crane operators from their cabins. The approaches to Ukraine's major ports are described as nearly devoid of shipping traffic as a result of the sustained offensive.

The escalation carries significant economic consequences beyond Ukraine, as the country is a major global exporter of grain and other agricultural commodities. Workers at the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine report that some veterans say working at the port feels more dangerous than front-line service. The intensification of Black Sea strikes represents a distinct and expanding front in Russia's war effort, separate from ground operations, aimed at economic strangulation rather than territorial gains.
